 152	## 5. SOLID Design Principles Implementation ✅
 153	
 154	### Single Responsibility Principle ✅
 155	Each class has a single, well-defined responsibility:
 156	- `MessageProducer<T>`: Only responsible for message publishing
 157	- `MessageConsumer<T>`: Only responsible for message consumption
 158	- `SchemaMigrationManager`: Only responsible for database schema management
 159	- `HealthCheckManager`: Only responsible for health monitoring
 160	- `CircuitBreakerManager`: Only responsible for resilience patterns
 161	- `DeadLetterQueueManager`: Only responsible for failed message handling
 162	
 163	### Open/Closed Principle ✅
 164	The architecture is open for extension but closed for modification:
 165	- `QueueFactory` interface allows new queue implementations
 166	- `QueueFactoryProvider` enables pluggable queue types
 167	- Abstract provider interfaces in `peegeeq-api` for extensibility
 168	- Configuration-driven queue type selection
 169	
 170	### Liskov Substitution Principle ✅
 171	Subtypes are fully substitutable for their base types:
 172	- All queue factories implement the `QueueFactory` interface
 173	- All producers implement `MessageProducer<T>`
 174	- All consumers implement `MessageConsumer<T>`
 175	- Provider implementations are interchangeable through interfaces
 176	
 177	### Interface Segregation Principle ✅
 178	Interfaces are client-specific and focused:
 179	- Separate `MessageProducer<T>` and `MessageConsumer<T>` interfaces
 180	- Specialized provider interfaces (`ConnectionProvider`, `MetricsProvider`, etc.)
 181	- Focused configuration interfaces for different concerns
 182	
 183	### Dependency Inversion Principle ✅
 184	High-level modules depend on abstractions, not concretions:
 185	- All modules depend on interfaces defined in `peegeeq-api`
 186	- `DatabaseService` abstraction hides database implementation details
 187	- Factory pattern with `QueueFactoryProvider` eliminates direct dependencies
 188	- Configuration injection through interfaces

 190	## 6. Thread Safety Implementation ✅
 191	
 192	### 6.1 Database-Level Concurrency Control ✅
 193	- **Advisory locks**: Implemented for preventing duplicate message processing
 194	- **Row-level locking**: Used in queue operations for message visibility
 195	- **Visibility timeout**: Automatic message release after timeout expiration
 196	- **Lock expiration**: Background cleanup of expired locks
 197	- **Transactional consistency**: ACID guarantees for all operations
 198	
 199	### 6.2 Application-Level Thread Safety ✅
 200	- **Immutable message objects**: All message implementations are immutable
 201	- **Thread-safe connection pool**: HikariCP provides thread-safe connection management
 202	- **Concurrent processing**: Vert.x-based async processing with proper synchronization
 203	- **Atomic operations**: Java concurrency utilities for state management
 204	- **Thread confinement**: Stateful components properly confined to threads
 205	
 206	### 6.3 Scaling and Performance ✅
 207	- **Configurable worker pools**: Thread count configuration for different workloads
 208	- **Backpressure management**: Adaptive flow control and rate limiting
 209	- **Circuit breakers**: Automatic failure detection and recovery
 210	- **Connection pooling**: Efficient resource utilization with HikariCP
 211	- **Horizontal scaling**: Multiple consumer instances supported

message handling\n\n### Open/Closed Principle\nThe architecture is open for extension but closed for modification:\n- `QueueFactory` interface allows new queue implementations\n- `EventStore<T>` Interface Segregation Principle\nInterfaces are client-specific and focused:\n- Separate `MessageProducer<T>` and `MessageConsumer<T>` interfaces\n- Dedicated `EventStore<T>` interface for bi-temporal operations\n- Specialized provider interfaces for different concerns\n- Focused configuration interfaces for different components\n\n### Dependency Inversion Principle\nHigh-level modules depend on abstractions, not concretions:\n- All modules depend on interfaces defined in `peegeeq-api`\n- `DatabaseService` abstraction hides database implementation details\n- Factory pattern with  1	# PeeGeeQ Technical Architecture
 2	
 3	## Overview
 4	
 5	PeeGeeQ is a production-ready, enterprise-grade message queue system built on PostgreSQL, providing both native queue functionality and outbox pattern implementation. The system leverages PostgreSQL's advanced features including LISTEN/NOTIFY, advisory locks, and ACID transactions to deliver reliable, scalable message processing.
 6	
 7	## System Architecture
 8	
 9	### Core Components
 10

 12	┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 13	│ PeeGeeQ System │
 14	├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

 19	│ │ • MessageConsumer│ │ LISTEN/NOTIFY │ │ Management│ │
 20	│ │ • Message │ │ • Advisory Locks│ │ • Migrations│ │
 21	│ │ • Interfaces │ │ • Visibility │ │ • Health │ │
 22	│ │ │ │ Timeout │ │ Checks │ │
 23	│ └─────────────────┘ │ • Dead Letter │ │ • Metrics │ │
 24	│ │ Queue │ │ • Circuit │ │
 25	│ ┌─────────────────┐ │ • Metrics │ │ Breakers │ │
 26	│ │ PeeGeeQ Outbox │ │ Integration │ │ │ │
 27	│ │ │ └─────────────────┘ └─────────────┘ │
 28	│ │ • Outbox Pattern│ │

 35	
 36	### Module Structure
 37	
 38	#### 1. **peegeeq-api** - Core Interfaces
 39	- `MessageProducer<T>` - Message publishing interface
 40	- `MessageConsumer<T>` - Message consumption interface 
 41	- `Message<T>` - Message abstraction
 42	- Common data structures and contracts
 43	
 44	#### 2. **peegeeq-db** - Database Foundation
 45	- Connection management with HikariCP
 46	- Schema migrations with Flyway
 47	- Health checks and monitoring
 48	- Metrics collection
 49	- Circuit breaker patterns
 50	- Dead letter queue management
 51	
 52	#### 3. **peegeeq-native** - Native Queue Implementation
 53	- Real-time message processing with LISTEN/NOTIFY
 54	- Advisory locks for concurrency control
 55	- Visibility timeout for message reliability
 56	- Dead letter queue integration
 57	- Comprehensive metrics tracking
 58	- Vert.x-based async processing
 59	
 60	#### 4. **peegeeq-outbox** - Outbox Pattern Implementation
 61	- Transactional outbox pattern
 62	- JDBC-based reliable messaging
 63	- Polling-based message processing
 64	- Integration with existing database transactions
 65	
 66	## Database Schema
 67	
 68	### Core Tables
 69	
 70	```sql
 71	-- Main message queue table
 72	CREATE TABLE queue_messages (
 73	 id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
 74	 topic VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
 75	 payload JSONB NOT NULL,
 76	 headers JSONB DEFAULT '{}',
 77	 correlation_id VARCHAR(255),
 78	 message_group VARCHAR(255),
 79	 status VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'AVAILABLE',
 80	 priority INTEGER DEFAULT 5,
 81	 retry_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
 82	 max_retries INTEGER DEFAULT 3,
 83	 lock_until TIMESTAMPTZ,
 84	 error_message TEXT,
 85	 created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
 86	 INDEX idx_queue_messages_topic_status (topic, status),
 87	 INDEX idx_queue_messages_lock_until (lock_until),
 88	 INDEX idx_queue_messages_priority_created (priority DESC, created_at ASC)
 89	);
 90	
 91	-- Outbox table for transactional messaging
 92	CREATE TABLE outbox (
 93	 id VARCHAR(255) PRIMARY KEY,
 94	 topic VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
 95	 payload JSONB NOT NULL,
 96	 headers JSONB DEFAULT '{}',
 97	 correlation_id VARCHAR(255),
 98	 message_group VARCHAR(255),
 99	 status VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'PENDING',
 100	 processing_started_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
 101	 created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
 102	 INDEX idx_outbox_topic_status (topic, status),
 103	 INDEX idx_outbox_created_at (created_at)
 104	);
 105	
 106	-- Dead letter queue for failed messages
 107	CREATE TABLE dead_letter_queue (
 108	 id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
 109	 original_table VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
 110	 original_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
 111	 topic VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
 112	 payload JSONB NOT NULL,
 113	 headers JSONB DEFAULT '{}',
 114	 correlation_id VARCHAR(255),
 115	 message_group VARCHAR(255),
 116	 retry_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
 117	 failure_reason TEXT,
 118	 failed_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
 119	 original_created_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
 120	 INDEX idx_dlq_topic (topic),
 121	 INDEX idx_dlq_failed_at (failed_at)
 122	);
 123	```
 124	
 125	## Key Features
 126	
 127	### 1. Real-time Message Processing
 128	- **LISTEN/NOTIFY**: Immediate message delivery using PostgreSQL's pub/sub
 129	- **Zero Polling**: Messages are pushed to consumers instantly
 130	- **Channel Management**: Automatic channel subscription and cleanup
 131	
 132	### 2. Concurrency Control
 133	- **Advisory Locks**: Prevents duplicate message processing
 134	- **Visibility Timeout**: Automatic message release after timeout
 135	- **Lock Expiration**: Background cleanup of expired locks
 136	
 137	### 3. Reliability & Resilience
 138	- **Dead Letter Queue**: Failed messages moved to DLQ after retry limit
 139	- **Circuit Breakers**: Automatic failure detection and recovery
 140	- **Health Checks**: Continuous system health monitoring
 141	- **Backpressure**: Automatic load management
 142	
 143	### 4. Observability
 144	- **Comprehensive Metrics**: Message lifecycle tracking
 145	- **Performance Monitoring**: Processing time and throughput metrics
 146	- **Error Tracking**: Detailed failure analysis
 147	- **Health Dashboards**: Real-time system status
 148	
 149	### 5. Transactional Guarantees
 150	- **Outbox Pattern**: Ensures message delivery with database transactions
 151	- **ACID Compliance**: Full transactional consistency
 152	- **Exactly-Once Processing**: Prevents message duplication
 153	
 154	## Performance Characteristics
 155	
 156	### Throughput
 157	- **Native Queue**: 10,000+ messages/second
 158	- **Outbox Pattern**: 5,000+ messages/second
 159	- **Concurrent Consumers**: Scales linearly with consumer count
 160	
 161	### Latency
 162	- **Real-time Delivery**: <10ms with LISTEN/NOTIFY
 163	- **Polling-based**: 2-5 seconds (configurable)
 164	- **Processing Overhead**: <1ms per message
 165	
 166	### Scalability
 167	- **Horizontal Scaling**: Multiple consumer instances
 168	- **Vertical Scaling**: Leverages PostgreSQL performance
 169	- **Connection Pooling**: Efficient resource utilization
 170	
 171	## Configuration
 172	
 173	### Database Connection
 174	```properties
 175	peegeeq.database.host=localhost
 176	peegeeq.database.port=5432
 177	peegeeq.database.name=peegeeq
 178	peegeeq.database.username=peegeeq
 179	peegeeq.database.password=peegeeq
 180	peegeeq.database.ssl.enabled=true
 181	```
 182	
 183	### Connection Pool
 184	```properties
 185	peegeeq.pool.minimum-idle=5
 186	peegeeq.pool.maximum-pool-size=20
 187	peegeeq.pool.connection-timeout=30000
 188	peegeeq.pool.idle-timeout=600000
 189	peegeeq.pool.max-lifetime=1800000
 190	```
 191	
 192	### Queue Configuration
 193	```properties
 194	peegeeq.queue.visibility-timeout=PT30S
 195	peegeeq.queue.max-retries=3
 196	peegeeq.queue.dead-letter.enabled=true
 197	peegeeq.queue.metrics.enabled=true
 198	```
 199	
 200	## Technology Stack
 201	
 202	### Core Technologies
 203	- **Java 21**: Modern Java features and performance
 204	- **PostgreSQL 15+**: Advanced database features
 205	- **Vert.x 4.5.11**: Reactive, non-blocking I/O
 206	- **HikariCP**: High-performance connection pooling
 207	- **Jackson**: JSON serialization/deserialization
 208	
 209	### Testing & Quality
 210	- **JUnit 5**: Modern testing framework
 211	- **TestContainers**: Integration testing with real PostgreSQL
 212	- **Maven**: Build and dependency management
 213	- **SLF4J + Logback**: Structured logging
 214	
 215	### Monitoring & Observability
 216	- **Micrometer**: Metrics collection
 217	- **Health Checks**: System health monitoring
 218	- **Circuit Breakers**: Resilience patterns
 219	- **Structured Logging**: Comprehensive observability
 220	
 221	## Deployment Considerations
 222	
 223	### Database Requirements
 224	- PostgreSQL 15+ recommended
 225	- Sufficient connection pool sizing
 226	- Proper indexing for performance
 227	- Regular maintenance and monitoring
 228	
 229	### Application Requirements
 230	- Java 21+ runtime
 231	- Adequate heap sizing for message processing
 232	- Network connectivity to PostgreSQL
 233	- Monitoring and alerting setup
 234	
 235	### Security
 236	- Database connection encryption (SSL/TLS)
 237	- Authentication and authorization
 238	- Network security (VPC, firewalls)
 239	- Audit logging for compliance
 240	
 241	## Next Steps
 242	
 243	This architecture provides a solid foundation for enterprise message processing. Future enhancements may include:
 244	
 245	- Message routing and filtering
 246	- Schema evolution support
 247	- Multi-tenant capabilities
 248	- Cloud-native deployment patterns
 249	- Advanced monitoring dashboards

 1	# PeeGeeQ Bi-Temporal Event Store
 2	
 3	The PeeGeeQ Bi-Temporal Event Store provides append-only, bi-temporal event storage with real-time processing capabilities. This module extends PeeGeeQ's PostgreSQL-based message queue system with sophisticated temporal event sourcing features.
 4	
 5	## Features
 6	
 7	### Core Capabilities
 8	- **Append-only**: Events are never deleted, only new versions added
 9	- **Bi-temporal**: Track both when events happened (valid time) and when they were recorded (transaction time)
 10	- **Real-time**: Immediate processing via PeeGeeQ's LISTEN/NOTIFY mechanism
 11	- **Historical**: Query any point-in-time view of your data
 12	- **Type safety**: Strongly typed events with JSON storage flexibility

 23	 * Represents a bi-temporal event in the append-only log store.
 24	 * 
 25	 * Bi-temporal events track two time dimensions:
 26	 * - Valid Time: When the event actually happened in the real world
 27	 * - Transaction Time: When the event was recorded in the system
 28	 * 
 29	 * This interface is part of the PeeGeeQ message queue system, providing
 30	 * production-ready PostgreSQL-based message queuing capabilities with
 31	 * bi-temporal event sourcing support.
 32	 * 
 33	 * @param <T> The type of event payload
 34	 * @author Mark Andrew Ray-Smith Cityline Ltd
 35	 * @since 2025-07-15
 36	 * @version 1.0
 37	 */
 38	public interface BiTemporalEvent<T> {
 39	 
 40	 /**
 41	 * Gets the unique identifier of the event.
 42	 * This ID is immutable and unique across all events.
 43	 *
 44	 * @return The event ID
 45	 */
 46	 String getEventId();
 47	 
 48	 /**
 49	 * Gets the event type identifier.
 50	 * Used for type safety and deserialization.
 51	 *
 52	 * @return The event type
 53	 */
 54	 String getEventType();
 55	 
 56	 /**
 57	 * Gets the payload of the event.
 58	 *
 59	 * @return The event payload
 60	 */
 61	 T getPayload();
 62	 
 63	 /**
 64	 * Gets the valid time - when the event actually happened in the real world.
 65	 * This represents the business time of the event.
 66	 *
 67	 * @return The valid time timestamp
 68	 */
 69	 Instant getValidTime();
 70	 
 71	 /**
 72	 * Gets the transaction time - when the event was recorded in the system.
 73	 * This represents the system time when the event was persisted.
 74	 *
 75	 * @return The transaction time timestamp
 76	 */
 77	 Instant getTransactionTime();
 78	 
 79	 /**
 80	 * Gets the version number of this event.
 81	 * Used for tracking event evolution and corrections.
 82	 *
 83	 * @return The event version
 84	 */
 85	 long getVersion();
 86	 
 87	 /**
 88	 * Gets the ID of the previous version of this event, if any.
 89	 * Used for tracking event corrections and updates.
 90	 *
 91	 * @return The previous version ID, or null if this is the first version
 92	 */
 93	 String getPreviousVersionId();
 94

 96	 * Gets the headers associated with the event.
 97	 * Can contain metadata, correlation IDs, etc.
 98	 *
 99	 * @return The event headers
 100	 */
 101	 Map<String, String> getHeaders();

 103	 /**

 108	 String getCorrelationId();

 1	# PeeGeeQ Technical Architecture
 2	
 3	## Overview
 4	
 5	PeeGeeQ is a production-ready, enterprise-grade message queue system built on PostgreSQL, providing both native queue functionality and outbox pattern implementation. The system leverages PostgreSQL's advanced features including LISTEN/NOTIFY, advisory locks, and ACID transactions to deliver reliable, scalable message processing.
 6	
 7	## System Architecture
 8

 24	 BITEMPORAL[peegeeq-bitemporal<br/>Bi-temporal Event Store<br/>Append-only log<br/>Historical queries]

 458	### Clean Module Boundaries
 459	- **Dependency Inversion**: Implementation modules depend on abstractions

 471	- **Event Sourcing**: Complete audit trail with bi-temporal dimensions

 473	- **Real-time Processing**: Immediate event notifications

 2	# PostgreSQL as a Message Queue: Project Implementation Status
 3	
 4	## 1. Overview
 5	
 6	**Status: ✅ IMPLEMENTED AND PRODUCTION-READY**
 7	
 8	This document describes the completed Java-based implementation that demonstrates how to use PostgreSQL as a message queue. The project successfully showcases two primary approaches with enterprise-grade production readiness features:
 9	
 10	1. **Outbox Pattern**: A reliable way to implement eventual consistency in distributed systems
 11	2. **Native PostgreSQL Queue**: Utilizing PostgreSQL's LISTEN/NOTIFY, advisory locks, and other features
 12	
 13	The implementation adheres to SOLID design principles, ensures thread safety throughout, and includes comprehensive production readiness features including database schema management, monitoring, health checks, circuit breakers, and resilience patterns.
 14	
 15	## 2. Project Status
 16	
 17	**Current State**: The project has been fully implemented with the following major components:
 18	
 19	- ✅ **Multi-module Maven architecture** with clear separation of concerns
 20	- ✅ **Production-ready database schema management** with versioned migrations
 21	- ✅ **Comprehensive metrics and monitoring** with Micrometer integration
 22	- ✅ **Externalized configuration management** with environment-specific profiles
 23	- ✅ **Health checks and resilience patterns** including circuit breakers and backpressure management
 24	- ✅ **Dead letter queue implementation** for failed message handling
 25	- ✅ **Extensive test coverage** with TestContainers integration testing
 26	- ✅ **Self-contained demo applications** showcasing all features
 27	
 28	## 3. Implemented Approaches

 30	### 3.1 Outbox Pattern Implementation ✅
 31	
 32	**Implementation Status**: Fully implemented in `peegeeq-outbox` module
 33	
 34	**Features Implemented**:
 35	- Transactional message storage with ACID guarantees
 36	- JDBC-based reliable messaging
 37	- Integration with existing database transactions
 38	- Dead letter queue support for failed messages
 39	- Comprehensive metrics and monitoring

 152	## 5. SOLID Design Principles Implementation ✅
 153	
 154	### Single Responsibility Principle ✅
 155	Each class has a single, well-defined responsibility:
 156	- `MessageProducer<T>`: Only responsible for message publishing
 157	- `MessageConsumer<T>`: Only responsible for message consumption
 158	- `SchemaMigrationManager`: Only responsible for database schema management
 159	- `HealthCheckManager`: Only responsible for health monitoring
 160	- `CircuitBreakerManager`: Only responsible for resilience patterns
 161	- `DeadLetterQueueManager`: Only responsible for failed message handling
 162	
 163	### Open/Closed Principle ✅
 164	The architecture is open for extension but closed for modification:
 165	- `QueueFactory` interface allows new queue implementations
 166	- `QueueFactoryProvider` enables pluggable queue types
 167	- Abstract provider interfaces in `peegeeq-api` for extensibility
 168	- Configuration-driven queue type selection
 169	
 170	### Liskov Substitution Principle ✅
 171	Subtypes are fully substitutable for their base types:
 172	- All queue factories implement the `QueueFactory` interface
 173	- All producers implement `MessageProducer<T>`
 174	- All consumers implement `MessageConsumer<T>`
 175	- Provider implementations are interchangeable through interfaces
 176	
 177	### Interface Segregation Principle ✅
 178	Interfaces are client-specific and focused:
 179	- Separate `MessageProducer<T>` and `MessageConsumer<T>` interfaces
 180	- Specialized provider interfaces (`ConnectionProvider`, `MetricsProvider`, etc.)
 181	- Focused configuration interfaces for different concerns
 182	
 183	### Dependency Inversion Principle ✅
 184	High-level modules depend on abstractions, not concretions:
 185	- All modules depend on interfaces defined in `peegeeq-api`
 186	- `DatabaseService` abstraction hides database implementation details
 187	- Factory pattern with `QueueFactoryProvider` eliminates direct dependencies
 188	- Configuration injection through interfaces
 189	
 190	## 6. Thread Safety Implementation ✅
 191	
 192	### 6.1 Database-Level Concurrency Control ✅
 193	- **Advisory locks**: Implemented for preventing duplicate message processing
 194	- **Row-level locking**: Used in queue operations for message visibility
 195	- **Visibility timeout**: Automatic message release after timeout expiration
 196	- **Lock expiration**: Background cleanup of expired locks
 197	- **Transactional consistency**: ACID guarantees for all operations
 198	
 199	### 6.2 Application-Level Thread Safety ✅
 200	- **Immutable message objects**: All message implementations are immutable
 201	- **Thread-safe connection pool**: HikariCP provides thread-safe connection management
 202	- **Concurrent processing**: Vert.x-based async processing with proper synchronization
 203	- **Atomic operations**: Java concurrency utilities for state management
 204	- **Thread confinement**: Stateful components properly confined to threads
 205	
 206	### 6.3 Scaling and Performance ✅
 207	- **Configurable worker pools**: Thread count configuration for different workloads
 208	- **Backpressure management**: Adaptive flow control and rate limiting
 209	- **Circuit breakers**: Automatic failure detection and recovery
 210	- **Connection pooling**: Efficient resource utilization with HikariCP
 211	- **Horizontal scaling**: Multiple consumer instances supported
 212

 215	### 7.1 Database Schema Management ✅
 216	**Implemented with versioned migrations using custom migration manager**
 217	
 218	```sql
 219	-- Main message queue table (V001__Create_Base_Tables.sql)
 220	CREATE TABLE queue_messages (
 221	 id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
 222	 topic VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
 223	 payload JSONB NOT NULL,
 224	 headers JSONB DEFAULT '{}',
 225	 correlation_id VARCHAR(255),
 226	 message_group VARCHAR(255),
 227	 status VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'AVAILABLE',
 228	 priority INTEGER DEFAULT 5,
 229	 retry_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
 230	 max_retries INTEGER DEFAULT 3,
 231	 lock_until TIMESTAMPTZ,
 232	 error_message TEXT,
 233	 created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
 234	);
 235	
 236	-- Outbox table for transactional messaging
 237	CREATE TABLE outbox (
 238	 id VARCHAR(255) PRIMARY KEY,
 239	 topic VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
 240	 payload JSONB NOT NULL,
 241	 headers JSONB DEFAULT '{}',
 242	 correlation_id VARCHAR(255),
 243	 message_group VARCHAR(255),
 244	 status VARCHAR(50) DEFAULT 'PENDING',
 245	 processing_started_at TIMESTAMPTZ,
 246	 created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
 247	);
 248	
 249	-- Dead letter queue for failed messages
 250	CREATE TABLE dead_letter_queue (
 251	 id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
 252	 original_table VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
 253	 original_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
 254	 topic VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
 255	 payload JSONB NOT NULL,
 256	 headers JSONB DEFAULT '{}',
 257	 correlation_id VARCHAR(255),
 258	 message_group VARCHAR(255),
 259	 retry_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
 260	 failure_reason TEXT,
 261	 failed_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
 262	 original_created_at TIMESTAMPTZ
 263	);
 264	
 265	-- Performance indexes (V002__Add_Indexes.sql)
 266	CREATE INDEX idx_queue_messages_topic_status ON queue_messages(topic, status);
 267	CREATE INDEX idx_queue_messages_lock_until ON queue_messages(lock_until);
 268	CREATE INDEX idx_queue_messages_priority_created ON queue_messages(priority DESC, created_at ASC);
 269	CREATE INDEX idx_outbox_topic_status ON outbox(topic, status);
 270	CREATE INDEX idx_outbox_created_at ON outbox(created_at);
 271	CREATE INDEX idx_dlq_topic ON dead_letter_queue(topic);
 272	CREATE INDEX idx_dlq_failed_at ON dead_letter_queue(failed_at);
 273	```

 1	# PeeGeeQ - Getting Started Guide 
 2	#### © Mark Andrew Ray-Smith Cityline Ltd 2025
 3	
 4	Welcome to **PeeGeeQ** (PostgreSQL as a Message Queue) - a production-ready message queue system built on PostgreSQL that provides both high-performance real-time messaging and transactional messaging patterns.
 5	
 6	## What is PeeGeeQ?
 7	
 8	PeeGeeQ is an enterprise-grade message queue system that leverages PostgreSQL's advanced features to provide:
 9	
 10	- **Native Queue**: High-performance, real-time message processing (10,000+ msg/sec, <10ms latency)
 11	- **Outbox Pattern**: Transactional messaging with database consistency guarantees (5,000+ msg/sec)
 12	- **Production Features**: Health checks, metrics, circuit breakers, dead letter queues, and more
 13	
 14	## Architecture Overview
 15	
 16	```mermaid
 17	graph TB
 18	 subgraph "Application Layer"
 19	 APP[Your Application<br/>Producer/Consumer Code]
 20	 end
 21	
 22	 subgraph "PeeGeeQ API Layer"
 23	 API[peegeeq-api<br/>MessageProducer<T><br/>MessageConsumer<T><br/>QueueFactory<br/>QueueFactoryProvider]
 24	 end
 25	
 26	 subgraph "Implementation Layer"
 27	 NATIVE[peegeeq-native<br/>Real-time LISTEN/NOTIFY<br/>10,000+ msg/sec<br/><10ms latency]
 28	 OUTBOX[peegeeq-outbox<br/>Transactional guarantees<br/>5,000+ msg/sec<br/>Polling-based]
 29	 end
 30	
 31	 subgraph "Database Layer"
 32	 DB[peegeeq-db<br/>PeeGeeQManager<br/>Schema Migrations<br/>Health Checks<br/>Metrics<br/>Circuit Breakers<br/>Dead Letter Queue]
 33	 end
 34	
 35	 subgraph "PostgreSQL Database"
 36	 POSTGRES[(PostgreSQL<br/>queue_messages<br/>outbox<br/>dead_letter_queue)]
 37	 end
 38	
 39	 APP --> API
 40	 API --> NATIVE
 41	 API --> OUTBOX
 42	 NATIVE --> DB
 43	 OUTBOX --> DB
 44	 DB --> POSTGRES
 45	```
 46	
 47	## System Requirements
 48	
 49	### Prerequisites
 50	
 51	- **Java**: JDK 21 or higher
 52	- **Maven**: 3.6 or higher
 53	- **Docker**: Required for self-contained demo (recommended for getting started)
 54	- **PostgreSQL**: 15+ (if not using Docker demo)
 55	
 56	### Dependencies
 57	
 58	PeeGeeQ automatically manages these dependencies:
 59	- PostgreSQL JDBC Driver (42.6.0)
 60	- HikariCP Connection Pooling (5.0.1)
 61	- Vert.x Async Framework (4.5.11)
 62	- Jackson JSON Processing (2.15.2)
 63	- Micrometer Metrics (1.12.0)
 64	- Resilience4j Circuit Breakers (2.1.0)
 65	
 66	## Quick Start (Recommended)
 67	
 68	The fastest way to get started is with our self-contained demo that requires no setup:
 69	
 70	### Option 1: Using Shell Scripts
 71	
 72	**Windows:**
 73	```cmd
 74	run-self-contained-demo.bat
 75	```
 76	
 77	**Unix/Linux/macOS:**
 78	```bash
 79	./run-self-contained-demo.sh
 80	```
 81	
 82	### Option 2: Using Maven Directly
 83	
 84	```bash
 85	mvn compile exec:java \
 86	 -Dexec.mainClass="dev.mars.peegeeq.examples.PeeGeeQSelfContainedDemo" \
 87	 -pl peegeeq-examples
 88	```
 89	
 90	This demo will:
 91	- Start a PostgreSQL container automatically
 92	- Demonstrate all PeeGeeQ production features
 93	- Show both Native and Outbox patterns
 94	- Clean up containers when finished
 95	- Require no external setup
 96	
 97	## Installation & Setup
 98	
 99	### Option 1: Using Published Maven Artifacts (Recommended)
 100	
 101	Add PeeGeeQ dependencies to your existing Maven project:
 102	
 103	```xml
 104	<properties>
 105	 <peegeeq.version>1.0.0</peegeeq.version>
 106	 <maven.compiler.source>21</maven.compiler.source>
 107	 <maven.compiler.target>21</maven.compiler.target>
 108	</properties>
 109	
 110	<dependencies>
 111	 <!-- PeeGeeQ Core Dependencies -->
 112	 <dependency>
 113	 <groupId>dev.mars</groupId>
 114	 <artifactId>peegeeq-api</artifactId>
 115	 <version>${peegeeq.version}</version>
 116	 </dependency>
 117	 <dependency>
 118	 <groupId>dev.mars</groupId>
 119	 <artifactId>peegeeq-db</artifactId>
 120	 <version>${peegeeq.version}</version>
 121	 </dependency>
 122	 <dependency>
 123	 <groupId>dev.mars</groupId>
 124	 <artifactId>peegeeq-native</artifactId>
 125	 <version>${peegeeq.version}</version>
 126	 </dependency>
 127	 <dependency>
 128	 <groupId>dev.mars</groupId>
 129	 <artifactId>peegeeq-outbox</artifactId>
 130	 <version>${peegeeq.version}</version>
 131	 </dependency>
 132	
 133	 <!-- Metrics (Optional but recommended) -->
 134	 <dependency>
 135	 <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
 136	 <artifactId>micrometer-core</artifactId>
 137	 <version>1.12.0</version>
 138	 </dependency>
 139	</dependencies>
 140	```
 141	
 142	### Option 2: Clone and Build from Source
 143	
 144	```bash
 145	git clone <repository-url>
 146	cd peegeeq
 147	mvn clean compile
 148	```
 149	
 150	### 3. Database Setup (If Not Using Docker Demo)
 151	
 152	#### Option A: Local PostgreSQL
 153	
 154	1. Install PostgreSQL 15+
 155	2. Create database and user:
 156	
 157	```sql
 158	CREATE DATABASE peegeeq;
 159	CREATE USER peegeeq WITH PASSWORD 'peegeeq';
 160	GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE peegeeq TO peegeeq;
 161	```
 162	
 163	#### Option B: Docker PostgreSQL
 164	
 165	```bash
 166	docker run -d \
 167	 --name peegeeq-postgres \
 168	 -e POSTGRES_DB=peegeeq \
 169	 -e POSTGRES_USER=peegeeq \
 170	 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=peegeeq \
 171	 -p 5432:5432 \
 172	 postgres:15
 173	```
 174	
 175	### 4. Run Traditional Example
 176	
 177	```bash
 178	# With default configuration
 179	java -cp <classpath> dev.mars.peegeeq.examples.PeeGeeQExample
 180	
 181	# With specific profile
 182	java -Dpeegeeq.profile=production -cp <classpath> dev.mars.peegeeq.examples.PeeGeeQExample
 183	```
 184	
 185	## Basic Usage
 186	
 187	### Complete Example: Simple Producer and Consumer
 188	
 189	Here's a complete example showing how to create a simple producer and consumer using the published PeeGeeQ artifacts:
 190	
 191	#### 1. Create a new Maven project with this pom.xml:
 192	
 193	```xml
 194	<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
 195	<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
 196	 xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
 197	 xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0
 198	 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
 199	 <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
 200	
 201	 <groupId>com.example</groupId>
 202	 <artifactId>my-peegeeq-app</artifactId>
 203	 <version>1.0.0</version>
 204	
 205	 <properties>
 206	 <maven.compiler.source>21</maven.compiler.source>
 207	 <maven.compiler.target>21</maven.compiler.target>
 208	 <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
 209	 <peegeeq.version>1.0.0</peegeeq.version>
 210	 </properties>
 211	
 212	 <dependencies>
 213	 <!-- PeeGeeQ Dependencies -->
 214	 <dependency>
 215	 <groupId>dev.mars</groupId>
 216	 <artifactId>peegeeq-api</artifactId>
 217	 <version>${peegeeq.version}</version>
 218	 </dependency>
 219	 <dependency>
 220	 <groupId>dev.mars</groupId>
 221	 <artifactId>peegeeq-db</artifactId>
 222	 <version>${peegeeq.version}</version>
 223	 </dependency>
 224	 <dependency>
 225	 <groupId>dev.mars</groupId>
 226	 <artifactId>peegeeq-native</artifactId>
 227	 <version>${peegeeq.version}</version>
 228	 </dependency>
 229	
 230	 <!-- Metrics -->
 231	 <dependency>
 232	 <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
 233	 <artifactId>micrometer-core</artifactId>
 234	 <version>1.12.0</version>
 235	 </dependency>
 236	
 237	 <!-- Logging -->
 238	 <dependency>
 239	 <groupId>ch.qos.logback</groupId>
 240	 <artifactId>logback-classic</artifactId>
 241	 <version>1.4.11</version>
 242	 </dependency>
 243	 </dependencies>
 244	</project>
 245	```
 246	
 247	#### 2. Create your application class:
 248	
 249	```java
 250	package com.example;
 251	
 252	import dev.mars.peegeeq.api.*;
 253	import dev.mars.peegeeq.db.PeeGeeQManager;
 254	import dev.mars.peegeeq.db.config.PeeGeeQConfiguration;
 255	import dev.mars.peegeeq.db.provider.PgDatabaseService;
 256	import dev.mars.peegeeq.db.provider.PgQueueFactoryProvider;
 257	import io.micrometer.core.instrument.simple.SimpleMeterRegistry;
 258	import org.slf4j.Logger;
 259	import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
 260	
 261	public class MyPeeGeeQApp {
 262	 private static final Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(MyPeeGeeQApp.class);
 263	
 264	 public static void main(String[] args) {
 265	 // Initialize PeeGeeQ Manager
 266	 try (PeeGeeQManager manager = new PeeGeeQManager(
 267	 new PeeGeeQConfiguration("development"),
 268	 new SimpleMeterRegistry())) {
 269	
 270	 // Start all services
 271	 manager.start();
 272	 logger.info("PeeGeeQ Manager started successfully");
 273	
 274	 // Create database service and factory provider
 275	 DatabaseService databaseService = new PgDatabaseService(manager);
 276	 QueueFactoryProvider provider = new PgQueueFactoryProvider();
 277	
 278	 // Create native queue factory for high-performance messaging
 279	 QueueFactory nativeFactory = provider.createNativeQueueFactory(databaseService);
 280	
 281	 // Create producer and consumer
 282	 MessageProducer<String> producer = nativeFactory.createProducer("my-topic", String.class);
 283	 MessageConsumer<String> consumer = nativeFactory.createConsumer("my-topic", String.class);
 284	
 285	 // Start consumer in background thread
 286	 Thread consumerThread = new Thread(() -> {
 287	 consumer.consume(message -> {
 288	 logger.info("Received message: {}", message.getPayload());
 289	 return true; // Acknowledge message
 290	 });
 291	 });
 292	 consumerThread.start();
 293	
 294	 // Send some messages
 295	 for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
 296	 String message = "Hello PeeGeeQ #" + i;
 297	 producer.send(message);
 298	 logger.info("Sent message: {}", message);
 299	 Thread.sleep(1000); // Wait 1 second between messages
 300	 }
 301	
 302	 // Wait a bit for messages to be processed
 303	 Thread.sleep(5000);
 304	
 305	 logger.info("Application completed successfully");
 306	
 307	 } catch (Exception e) {
 308	 logger.error("Application failed", e);
 309	 System.exit(1);
 310	 }
 311	 }
 312	}
 313	```
 314	
 315	#### 3. Create configuration file (src/main/resources/peegeeq-development.properties):
 316	
 317	```properties
 318	# Database Configuration
 319	peegeeq.database.host=localhost
 320	peegeeq.database.port=5432
 321	peegeeq.database.name=peegeeq
 322	peegeeq.database.username=peegeeq
 323	peegeeq.database.password=peegeeq
 324	
 325	# Connection Pool
 326	peegeeq.database.pool.min-size=2
 327	peegeeq.database.pool.max-size=5
 328	
 329	# Queue Settings
 330	peegeeq.queue.max-retries=3
 331	peegeeq.queue.visibility-timeout=PT30S
 332	
 333	# Enable features
 334	peegeeq.metrics.enabled=true
 335	peegeeq.health.enabled=true
 336	```
 337	
 338	#### 4. Run your application:
 339	
 340	```bash
 341	# Ensure PostgreSQL is running (or use Docker)
 342	docker run -d --name peegeeq-postgres \
 343	 -e POSTGRES_DB=peegeeq \
 344	 -e POSTGRES_USER=peegeeq \
 345	 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=peegeeq \
 346	 -p 5432:5432 \
 347	 postgres:15

 349	# Compile and run
 350	mvn compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass="com.example.MyPeeGeeQApp"
 351	```

 353	### Initialize PeeGeeQ Manager
 354	
 355	```java
 356	import dev.mars.peegeeq.db.PeeGeeQManager;
 357	import dev.mars.peegeeq.db.config.PeeGeeQConfiguration;
 358	import io.micrometer.core.instrument.simple.SimpleMeterRegistry;
 359	
 360	// Initialize with configuration profile
 361	PeeGeeQManager manager = new PeeGeeQManager(
 362	 new PeeGeeQConfiguration("development"),
 363	 new SimpleMeterRegistry()
 364	);
 365	
 366	// Start all services
 367	manager.start();
 368	```
 369	
 370	### Native Queue - High Performance Real-time
 371	
 372	```java
 373	import dev.mars.peegeeq.api.*;
 374	import dev.mars.peegeeq.db.provider.PgDatabaseService;
 375	import dev.mars.peegeeq.db.provider.PgQueueFactoryProvider;
 376	
 377	// Create database service and factory provider
 378	DatabaseService databaseService = new PgDatabaseService(manager);
 379	QueueFactoryProvider provider = new PgQueueFactoryProvider();
 380	
 381	// Create native queue factory
 382	QueueFactory nativeFactory = provider.createNativeQueueFactory(databaseService);
 383	
 384	// Create producer and consumer
 385	MessageProducer<String> producer = nativeFactory.createProducer("my-topic", String.class);
 386	MessageConsumer<String> consumer = nativeFactory.createConsumer("my-topic", String.class);
 387	
 388	// Send messages
 389	producer.send("Hello, PeeGeeQ!");
 390	
 391	// Consume messages
 392	consumer.consume(message -> {
 393	 System.out.println("Received: " + message.getPayload());
 394	 return true; // Acknowledge message
 395	});
 396	```
 397	
 398	### Outbox Pattern - Transactional Guarantees
 399	
 400	```java
 401	// Create outbox queue factory
 402	QueueFactory outboxFactory = provider.createOutboxQueueFactory(databaseService);
 403	
 404	// Create producer and consumer
 405	MessageProducer<String> outboxProducer = outboxFactory.createProducer("my-outbox-topic", String.class);
 406	MessageConsumer<String> outboxConsumer = outboxFactory.createConsumer("my-outbox-topic", String.class);
 407	
 408	// Send messages with transactional guarantees
 409	outboxProducer.send("Transactional message");
 410	
 411	// Consume messages
 412	outboxConsumer.consume(message -> {
 413	 System.out.println("Received transactional: " + message.getPayload());
 414	 return true;
 415	});
 416	```

 418	## Configuration
 419	
 420	### Environment Profiles
 421	
 422	PeeGeeQ supports multiple configuration profiles:
 423	
 424	- `development` - Default settings for local development
 425	- `production` - Optimized for production environments
 426	- `test` - Configured for testing scenarios
 427	
 428	### Configuration Files
 429	
 430	Configuration is loaded from:
 431	1. `peegeeq-default.properties` (base configuration)
 432	2. `peegeeq-{profile}.properties` (profile-specific overrides)
 433	3. System properties (highest priority)
 434	4. Environment variables
 435	
 436	### Key Configuration Properties
 437	
 438	```properties
 439	# Database Configuration
 440	peegeeq.database.host=localhost
 441	peegeeq.database.port=5432
 442	peegeeq.database.name=peegeeq
 443	peegeeq.database.username=peegeeq
 444	peegeeq.database.password=peegeeq
 445	
 446	# Connection Pool
 447	peegeeq.database.pool.min-size=5
 448	peegeeq.database.pool.max-size=10
 449	
 450	# Queue Settings
 451	peegeeq.queue.max-retries=3
 452	peegeeq.queue.visibility-timeout=PT30S
 453	peegeeq.queue.dead-letter.enabled=true
 454	
 455	# Metrics & Monitoring
 456	peegeeq.metrics.enabled=true
 457	peegeeq.health.enabled=true
 458	peegeeq.circuit-breaker.enabled=true
 459	```
 460	
 461	## Module Structure
 462	
 463	PeeGeeQ is organized into focused modules:
 464	
 465	- **peegeeq-api**: Core interfaces and contracts
 466	- **peegeeq-db**: Database management, migrations, health checks
 467	- **peegeeq-native**: High-performance LISTEN/NOTIFY implementation
 468	- **peegeeq-outbox**: Transactional outbox pattern implementation
 469	- **peegeeq-examples**: Self-contained demo applications
 470	
 471	## Production Features
 472	
 473	### Health Checks
 474	```java
 475	boolean healthy = manager.isHealthy();
 476	PeeGeeQManager.SystemStatus status = manager.getSystemStatus();
 477	```
 478	
 479	### Metrics Collection
 480	```java
 481	// Metrics are automatically collected and available via Micrometer
 482	// Integrate with Prometheus, Grafana, or other monitoring systems
 483	```
 484	
 485	### Circuit Breakers
 486	```java
 487	// Automatic circuit breaker protection for database operations
 488	// Configurable failure thresholds and recovery timeouts
 489	```
 490	
 491	### Dead Letter Queue
 492	```java
 493	// Failed messages automatically moved to dead letter queue
 494	// Supports message reprocessing and failure analysis
 495	```

 1	# PeeGeeQ Bi-Temporal Event Store
 2	
 3	The PeeGeeQ Bi-Temporal Event Store provides append-only, bi-temporal event storage with real-time processing capabilities. This module extends PeeGeeQ's PostgreSQL-based message queue system with sophisticated temporal event sourcing features.
 4	
 5	## Features
 6	
 7	### Core Capabilities
 8	- **Append-only**: Events are never deleted, only new versions added
 9	- **Bi-temporal**: Track both when events happened (valid time) and when they were recorded (transaction time)
 10	- **Real-time**: Immediate processing via PeeGeeQ's LISTEN/NOTIFY mechanism
 11	- **Historical**: Query any point-in-time view of your data
 12	- **Type safety**: Strongly typed events with JSON storage flexibility
 13	
 14	### Advanced Features
 15	- **Event Corrections**: Support for correcting historical events while maintaining audit trail
 16	- **Versioning**: Automatic version tracking for event evolution
 17	- **Temporal Queries**: Rich query capabilities across both time dimensions
 18	- **Real-time Subscriptions**: Subscribe to event streams with filtering
 19	- **Statistics**: Comprehensive metrics and monitoring
 20	
 21	## Quick Start
 22	
 23	### 1. Add Dependency
 24	
 25	```xml
 26	<dependency>
 27	 <groupId>dev.mars</groupId>
 28	 <artifactId>peegeeq-bitemporal</artifactId>
 29	 <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
 30	</dependency>
 31	```
 32	
 33	### 2. Create Event Store
 34	
 35	```java
 36	// Initialize PeeGeeQ
 37	PeeGeeQManager manager = new PeeGeeQManager();
 38	manager.start();
 39	
 40	// Create event store factory
 41	BiTemporalEventStoreFactory factory = new BiTemporalEventStoreFactory(manager);
 42	
 43	// Create event store for your event type
 44	EventStore<OrderEvent> eventStore = factory.createEventStore(OrderEvent.class);
 45	```
 46	
 47	### 3. Append Events
 48	
 49	```java
 50	// Create an event
 51	OrderEvent order = new OrderEvent("ORDER-001", "CUST-123", new BigDecimal("99.99"), "CREATED");
 52	
 53	// Append with valid time (when it actually happened)
 54	Instant validTime = Instant.now().minus(1, ChronoUnit.HOURS);
 55	BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent> event = eventStore.append(
 56	 "OrderCreated", 
 57	 order, 
 58	 validTime,
 59	 Map.of("source", "web", "region", "US"),
 60	 "correlation-123",
 61	 "ORDER-001"
 62	).join();
 63	```
 64	
 65	### 4. Query Events
 66	
 67	```java
 68	// Query all events
 69	List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> allEvents = eventStore.query(EventQuery.all()).join();
 70	
 71	// Query by event type
 72	List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> orderEvents = eventStore.query(
 73	 EventQuery.forEventType("OrderCreated")
 74	).join();
 75	
 76	// Query by aggregate
 77	List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> order1Events = eventStore.query(
 78	 EventQuery.forAggregate("ORDER-001")
 79	).join();
 80	
 81	// Temporal range query
 82	List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> recentEvents = eventStore.query(
 83	 EventQuery.builder()
 84	 .validTimeRange(TemporalRange.from(Instant.now().minus(24, ChronoUnit.HOURS)))
 85	 .sortOrder(EventQuery.SortOrder.VALID_TIME_DESC)
 86	 .limit(100)
 87	 .build()
 88	).join();
 89	```
 90	
 91	### 5. Event Corrections
 92	
 93	```java
 94	// Append a correction for a previous event
 95	OrderEvent correctedOrder = new OrderEvent("ORDER-001", "CUST-123", new BigDecimal("89.99"), "CREATED");
 96	
 97	BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent> correction = eventStore.appendCorrection(
 98	 originalEvent.getEventId(),
 99	 "OrderCreated",
 100	 correctedOrder,
 101	 validTime,
 102	 "Price correction due to discount"
 103	).join();
 104	
 105	// Get all versions of an event
 106	List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> versions = eventStore.getAllVersions(originalEvent.getEventId()).join();
 107	```
 108	
 109	### 6. Point-in-Time Queries
 110	
 111	```java
 112	// Get event as it existed at a specific transaction time
 113	Instant pointInTime = Instant.now().minus(1, ChronoUnit.HOURS);
 114	BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent> historicalEvent = eventStore.getAsOfTransactionTime(
 115	 eventId, 
 116	 pointInTime
 117	).join();
 118	
 119	// Query events as they were valid at a specific time
 120	List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> historicalView = eventStore.query(
 121	 EventQuery.asOfValidTime(pointInTime)
 122	).join();
 123	```
 124	
 125	### 7. Real-time Subscriptions
 126	
 127	```java
 128	// Subscribe to all events
 129	eventStore.subscribe(null, event -> {
 130	 System.out.println("New event: " + event.getEventType());
 131	 return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null);
 132	}).join();
 133	
 134	// Subscribe to specific event type
 135	eventStore.subscribe("OrderCreated", event -> {
 136	 System.out.println("New order: " + event.getPayload());
 137	 return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null);
 138	}).join();
 139	
 140	// Subscribe to events for specific aggregate
 141	eventStore.subscribe("OrderCreated", "ORDER-001", event -> {
 142	 System.out.println("Order 001 updated: " + event.getPayload());
 143	 return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null);
 144	}).join();
 145	```
 146	
 147	## Database Schema
 148	
 149	The bi-temporal event store uses a dedicated table with the following structure:
 150	
 151	```sql
 152	CREATE TABLE bitemporal_event_log (
 153	 id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
 154	 event_id VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
 155	 event_type VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
 156	 
 157	 -- Bi-temporal dimensions
 158	 valid_time TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NOT NULL,
 159	 transaction_time TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT NOW() NOT NULL,
 160	 
 161	 -- Event data
 162	 payload JSONB NOT NULL,
 163	 headers JSONB DEFAULT '{}',
 164	 
 165	 -- Versioning and corrections
 166	 version BIGINT DEFAULT 1 NOT NULL,
 167	 previous_version_id VARCHAR(255),
 168	 is_correction BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE NOT NULL,
 169	 correction_reason TEXT,
 170	 
 171	 -- Grouping and correlation
 172	 correlation_id VARCHAR(255),
 173	 aggregate_id VARCHAR(255),
 174	 
 175	 -- Metadata
 176	 created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT NOW() NOT NULL
 177	);
 178	```
 179	
 180	## Temporal Concepts
 181	
 182	### Valid Time vs Transaction Time
 183	
 184	- **Valid Time**: When the event actually happened in the real world (business time)
 185	- **Transaction Time**: When the event was recorded in the system (system time)
 186	
 187	This bi-temporal approach allows you to:
 188	- Correct historical data while maintaining audit trails
 189	- Query data as it was known at any point in time
 190	- Handle late-arriving events correctly
 191	- Support regulatory compliance and auditing requirements
 192	
 193	### Event Versioning
 194	
 195	Events can be corrected by creating new versions:
 196	- Original event: version 1, is_correction = false
 197	- Correction: version 2, is_correction = true, previous_version_id = original_event_id
 198	- Each correction creates a new event with incremented version
 199

 205	## Integration with PeeGeeQ
 206	
 207	The bi-temporal event store integrates seamlessly with PeeGeeQ's infrastructure:
 208	- Uses PeeGeeQ's connection pooling and database management
 209	- Leverages PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY for real-time events
 210	- Integrates with PeeGeeQ's metrics and monitoring
 211	- Benefits from PeeGeeQ's resilience patterns (circuit breakers, backpressure)
 212	
 213	## Performance Considerations
 214	
 215	- Optimized indexes for temporal queries
 216	- Efficient JSON storage with PostgreSQL JSONB
 217	- Connection pooling for high throughput
 218	- Configurable query limits and pagination
 219	- Real-time notifications without polling overhead

","workspace_file_chunks":[]},{"status":"success","request_id":"2683fc2f-b8d2-4064-9c3c-1b258609e7e6","request_message":"","structured_output_nodes":[{"id":1,"type":5,"content":"","tool_use":{"tool_use_id":"toolu_vrtx_01AWrxQpsp4MRo2VTaEdJe4V","tool_name":"str-replace-editor","input_json":"{"command": "str_replace", "path": "docs/GETTING_STARTED_GUIDE.md", "instruction_reminder": "ALWAYS BREAK DOWN EDITS INTO SMALLER CHUNKS OF AT MOST 150 LINES EACH.", "old_str_1": "// Consume messages\noutboxConsumer.consume(message -> {\n System.out.println(\"Received transactional: \" + message.getPayload());\n return true;\n});\n```\n\n## Configuration", "old_str_start_line_number_1": 418, "old_str_end_line_number_1": 424, "new_str_1": "// Consume messages\noutboxConsumer.consume(message -> {\n System.out.println(\"Received transactional: \" + message.getPayload());\n return true;\n});\n```\n\n### Bi-Temporal Event Store - Append-Only Event Sourcing\n\n```java\nimport dev.mars.peegeeq.bitemporal.BiTemporalEventStoreFactory;\nimport dev.mars.peegeeq.bitemporal.EventStore;\nimport dev.mars.peegeeq.bitemporal.BiTemporalEvent;\nimport dev.mars.peegeeq.bitemporal.EventQuery;\n\n// Create event store factory\nBiTemporalEventStoreFactory factory = new BiTemporalEventStoreFactory(manager);\n\n// Create event store for your event type\nEventStore<OrderEvent> eventStore = factory.createEventStore(OrderEvent.class);\n\n// Append events with bi-temporal dimensions\nOrderEvent order = new OrderEvent(\"ORDER-001\", \"CUST-123\", new BigDecimal(\"99.99\"), \"CREATED\");\nInstant validTime = Instant.now().minus(1, ChronoUnit.HOURS); // When it actually happened\n\nBiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent> event = eventStore.append(\n \"OrderCreated\", \n order, \n validTime,\n Map.of(\"source\", \"web\", \"region\", \"US\"),\n \"correlation-123\",\n \"ORDER-001\"\n).join();\n\n// Query events by type, aggregate, or temporal ranges\nList<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> orderEvents = eventStore.query(\n EventQuery.forAggregate(\"ORDER-001\")\n).join();\n\n// Point-in-time queries - see data as it was at any moment\nInstant pointInTime = Instant.now().minus(1, ChronoUnit.HOURS);\nList<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> historicalView = eventStore.query(\n EventQuery.asOfValidTime(pointInTime)\n).join();\n\n// Real-time subscriptions to event streams\neventStore.subscribe(\"OrderCreated\", event -> {\n System.out.println(\"New order event: \" + event.getPayload());\n return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null);\n}).join();\n\n// Event corrections while maintaining audit trail\nOrderEvent correctedOrder = new OrderEvent(\"ORDER-001\", \"CUST-123\", new BigDecimal(\"89.99\"), \"CREATED\");\nBiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent> correction = eventStore.appendCorrection(\n event.getEventId(),\n \"OrderCreated\",\n correctedOrder,\n validTime,\n \"Price correction due to discount\"\n).join();\n```\n\n**Key Features:**\n- **Append-only**: Events are never deleted, only new versions added\n- **Bi-temporal**: Track both when events happened (valid time) and when recorded (transaction time)\n- **Real-time**: Immediate processing via PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY\n- **Historical**: Query any point-in-time view of your data\n- **Type safety**: Strongly typed events with JSON storage flexibility\n- **Event corrections**: Support for correcting historical events while maintaining audit trail\n\n## Configuration"}","mcp_server_name":"","mcp_tool_name":""}},{"id":2,"type":0,"content":"Now let's add a new section for the Bi-Temporal Event Store after the Outbox Pattern section:

 1	# PeeGeeQ - Getting Started Guide 
 2	#### © Mark Andrew Ray-Smith Cityline Ltd 2025
 3	
 4	Welcome to **PeeGeeQ** (PostgreSQL as a Message Queue) - a production-ready message queue system built on PostgreSQL that provides both high-performance real-time messaging and transactional messaging patterns.
 5	
 6	## What is PeeGeeQ?
 7	
 8	PeeGeeQ is an enterprise-grade message queue system that leverages PostgreSQL's advanced features to provide:
 9	
 10	- **Native Queue**: High-performance, real-time message processing (10,000+ msg/sec, <10ms latency)
 11	- **Outbox Pattern**: Transactional messaging with database consistency guarantees (5,000+ msg/sec)
 12	- **Production Features**: Health checks, metrics, circuit breakers, dead letter queues, and more
 13	
 14	## Architecture Overview
 15	
 16	```mermaid
 17	graph TB
 18	 subgraph "Application Layer"
 19	 APP[Your Application<br/>Producer/Consumer Code]
 20	 end
 21	
 22	 subgraph "PeeGeeQ API Layer"
 23	 API[peegeeq-api<br/>MessageProducer<T><br/>MessageConsumer<T><br/>QueueFactory<br/>QueueFactoryProvider]
 24	 end
 25	
 26	 subgraph "Implementation Layer"
 27	 NATIVE[peegeeq-native<br/>Real-time LISTEN/NOTIFY<br/>10,000+ msg/sec<br/><10ms latency]
 28	 OUTBOX[peegeeq-outbox<br/>Transactional guarantees<br/>5,000+ msg/sec<br/>Polling-based]
 29	 end
 30	
 31	 subgraph "Database Layer"
 32	 DB[peegeeq-db<br/>PeeGeeQManager<br/>Schema Migrations<br/>Health Checks<br/>Metrics<br/>Circuit Breakers<br/>Dead Letter Queue]
 33	 end
 34	
 35	 subgraph "PostgreSQL Database"
 36	 POSTGRES[(PostgreSQL<br/>queue_messages<br/>outbox<br/>dead_letter_queue)]
 37	 end
 38	
 39	 APP --> API
 40	 API --> NATIVE
 41	 API --> OUTBOX
 42	 NATIVE --> DB
 43	 OUTBOX --> DB
 44	 DB --> POSTGRES
 45	```
 46	
 47	## System Requirements
 48	
 49	### Prerequisites
 50	
 51	- **Java**: JDK 21 or higher
 52	- **Maven**: 3.6 or higher
 53	- **Docker**: Required for self-contained demo (recommended for getting started)
 54	- **PostgreSQL**: 15+ (if not using Docker demo)
 55	
 56	### Dependencies
 57	
 58	PeeGeeQ automatically manages these dependencies:
 59	- PostgreSQL JDBC Driver (42.6.0)
 60	- HikariCP Connection Pooling (5.0.1)
 61	- Vert.x Async Framework (4.5.11)
 62	- Jackson JSON Processing (2.15.2)
 63	- Micrometer Metrics (1.12.0)
 64	- Resilience4j Circuit Breakers (2.1.0)
 65	
 66	## Quick Start (Recommended)
 67	
 68	The fastest way to get started is with our self-contained demo that requires no setup:
 69	
 70	### Option 1: Using Shell Scripts
 71	
 72	**Windows:**
 73	```cmd
 74	run-self-contained-demo.bat
 75	```
 76	
 77	**Unix/Linux/macOS:**
 78	```bash
 79	./run-self-contained-demo.sh
 80	```
 81	
 82	### Option 2: Using Maven Directly
 83	
 84	```bash
 85	mvn compile exec:java \
 86	 -Dexec.mainClass="dev.mars.peegeeq.examples.PeeGeeQSelfContainedDemo" \
 87	 -pl peegeeq-examples
 88	```
 89	
 90	This demo will:
 91	- Start a PostgreSQL container automatically
 92	- Demonstrate all PeeGeeQ production features
 93	- Show both Native and Outbox patterns
 94	- Clean up containers when finished
 95	- Require no external setup
 96	
 97	## Installation & Setup
 98	
 99	### Option 1: Using Published Maven Artifacts (Recommended)
 100	
 101	Add PeeGeeQ dependencies to your existing Maven project:
 102	
 103	```xml
 104	<properties>
 105	 <peegeeq.version>1.0.0</peegeeq.version>
 106	 <maven.compiler.source>21</maven.compiler.source>
 107	 <maven.compiler.target>21</maven.compiler.target>
 108	</properties>
 109	
 110	<dependencies>
 111	 <!-- PeeGeeQ Core Dependencies -->
 112	 <dependency>
 113	 <groupId>dev.mars</groupId>
 114	 <artifactId>peegeeq-api</artifactId>
 115	 <version>${peegeeq.version}</version>
 116	 </dependency>
 117	 <dependency>
 118	 <groupId>dev.mars</groupId>
 119	 <artifactId>peegeeq-db</artifactId>
 120	 <version>${peegeeq.version}</version>
 121	 </dependency>
 122	 <dependency>
 123	 <groupId>dev.mars</groupId>
 124	 <artifactId>peegeeq-native</artifactId>
 125	 <version>${peegeeq.version}</version>
 126	 </dependency>
 127	 <dependency>
 128	 <groupId>dev.mars</groupId>
 129	 <artifactId>peegeeq-outbox</artifactId>
 130	 <version>${peegeeq.version}</version>
 131	 </dependency>
 132	
 133	 <!-- Metrics (Optional but recommended) -->
 134	 <dependency>
 135	 <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
 136	 <artifactId>micrometer-core</artifactId>
 137	 <version>1.12.0</version>
 138	 </dependency>
 139	</dependencies>
 140	```
 141	
 142	### Option 2: Clone and Build from Source
 143	
 144	```bash
 145	git clone <repository-url>
 146	cd peegeeq
 147	mvn clean compile
 148	```
 149	
 150	### 3. Database Setup (If Not Using Docker Demo)
 151	
 152	#### Option A: Local PostgreSQL
 153	
 154	1. Install PostgreSQL 15+
 155	2. Create database and user:

 247	#### 2. Create your application class:
 248	
 249	```java
 250	package com.example;
 251	
 252	import dev.mars.peegeeq.api.*;
 253	import dev.mars.peegeeq.db.PeeGeeQManager;
 254	import dev.mars.peegeeq.db.config.PeeGeeQConfiguration;
 255	import dev.mars.peegeeq.db.provider.PgDatabaseService;
 256	import dev.mars.peegeeq.db.provider.PgQueueFactoryProvider;
 257	import io.micrometer.core.instrument.simple.SimpleMeterRegistry;
 258	import org.slf4j.Logger;
 259	import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
 260	
 261	public class MyPeeGeeQApp {
 262	 private static final Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(MyPeeGeeQApp.class);
 263	
 264	 public static void main(String[] args) {
 265	 // Initialize PeeGeeQ Manager
 266	 try (PeeGeeQManager manager = new PeeGeeQManager(
 267	 new PeeGeeQConfiguration("development"),
 268	 new SimpleMeterRegistry())) {
 269	
 270	 // Start all services
 271	 manager.start();
 272	 logger.info("PeeGeeQ Manager started successfully");
 273	
 274	 // Create database service and factory provider
 275	 DatabaseService databaseService = new PgDatabaseService(manager);
 276	 QueueFactoryProvider provider = new PgQueueFactoryProvider();
 277	
 278	 // Create native queue factory for high-performance messaging
 279	 QueueFactory nativeFactory = provider.createNativeQueueFactory(databaseService);
 280	
 281	 // Create producer and consumer
 282	 MessageProducer<String> producer = nativeFactory.createProducer("my-topic", String.class);
 283	 MessageConsumer<String> consumer = nativeFactory.createConsumer("my-topic", String.class);
 284	
 285	 // Start consumer in background thread
 286	 Thread consumerThread = new Thread(() -> {
 287	 consumer.consume(message -> {
 288	 logger.info("Received message: {}", message.getPayload());
 289	 return true; // Acknowledge message
 290	 });
 291	 });
 292	 consumerThread.start();
 293	
 294	 // Send some messages
 295	 for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
 296	 String message = "Hello PeeGeeQ #" + i;
 297	 producer.send(message);
 298	 logger.info("Sent message: {}", message);
 299	 Thread.sleep(1000); // Wait 1 second between messages
 300	 }
 301	
 302	 // Wait a bit for messages to be processed
 303	 Thread.sleep(5000);
 304	
 305	 logger.info("Application completed successfully");
 306	
 307	 } catch (Exception e) {
 308	 logger.error("Application failed", e);
 309	 System.exit(1);
 310	 }
 311	 }
 312	}
 313	```

 370	### Native Queue - High Performance Real-time
 371	
 372	```java
 373	import dev.mars.peegeeq.api.*;
 374	import dev.mars.peegeeq.db.provider.PgDatabaseService;
 375	import dev.mars.peegeeq.db.provider.PgQueueFactoryProvider;
 376	
 377	// Create database service and factory provider
 378	DatabaseService databaseService = new PgDatabaseService(manager);
 379	QueueFactoryProvider provider = new PgQueueFactoryProvider();
 380	
 381	// Create native queue factory
 382	QueueFactory nativeFactory = provider.createNativeQueueFactory(databaseService);
 383	
 384	// Create producer and consumer
 385	MessageProducer<String> producer = nativeFactory.createProducer("my-topic", String.class);
 386	MessageConsumer<String> consumer = nativeFactory.createConsumer("my-topic", String.class);
 387	
 388	// Send messages
 389	producer.send("Hello, PeeGeeQ!");
 390	
 391	// Consume messages
 392	consumer.consume(message -> {
 393	 System.out.println("Received: " + message.getPayload());
 394	 return true; // Acknowledge message
 395	});
 396	```
 397	
 398	### Outbox Pattern - Transactional Guarantees
 399	
 400	```java
 401	// Create outbox queue factory
 402	QueueFactory outboxFactory = provider.createOutboxQueueFactory(databaseService);
 403	
 404	// Create producer and consumer
 405	MessageProducer<String> outboxProducer = outboxFactory.createProducer("my-outbox-topic", String.class);
 406	MessageConsumer<String> outboxConsumer = outboxFactory.createConsumer("my-outbox-topic", String.class);
 407	
 408	// Send messages with transactional guarantees
 409	outboxProducer.send("Transactional message");
 410	
 411	// Consume messages
 412	outboxConsumer.consume(message -> {
 413	 System.out.println("Received transactional: " + message.getPayload());
 414	 return true;
 415	});
 416	```

 418	## Configuration
 419	
 420	### Environment Profiles
 421	
 422	PeeGeeQ supports multiple configuration profiles:
 423	
 424	- `development` - Default settings for local development
 425	- `production` - Optimized for production environments
 426	- `test` - Configured for testing scenarios
 427	
 428	### Configuration Files
 429	
 430	Configuration is loaded from:
 431	1. `peegeeq-default.properties` (base configuration)
 432	2. `peegeeq-{profile}.properties` (profile-specific overrides)
 433	3. System properties (highest priority)
 434	4. Environment variables
 435

 1	# PeeGeeQ Bi-Temporal Event Store
 2	
 3	The PeeGeeQ Bi-Temporal Event Store provides append-only, bi-temporal event storage with real-time processing capabilities. This module extends PeeGeeQ's PostgreSQL-based message queue system with sophisticated temporal event sourcing features.
 4	
 5	## Features
 6	
 7	### Core Capabilities
 8	- **Append-only**: Events are never deleted, only new versions added
 9	- **Bi-temporal**: Track both when events happened (valid time) and when they were recorded (transaction time)
 10	- **Real-time**: Immediate processing via PeeGeeQ's LISTEN/NOTIFY mechanism
 11	- **Historical**: Query any point-in-time view of your data
 12	- **Type safety**: Strongly typed events with JSON storage flexibility
 13	
 14	### Advanced Features
 15	- **Event Corrections**: Support for correcting historical events while maintaining audit trail
 16	- **Versioning**: Automatic version tracking for event evolution
 17	- **Temporal Queries**: Rich query capabilities across both time dimensions
 18	- **Real-time Subscriptions**: Subscribe to event streams with filtering
 19	- **Statistics**: Comprehensive metrics and monitoring
 20	
 21	## Quick Start
 22	
 23	### 1. Add Dependency
 24	
 25	```xml
 26	<dependency>
 27	 <groupId>dev.mars</groupId>
 28	 <artifactId>peegeeq-bitemporal</artifactId>
 29	 <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
 30	</dependency>
 31	```
 32	
 33	### 2. Create Event Store
 34	
 35	```java
 36	// Initialize PeeGeeQ
 37	PeeGeeQManager manager = new PeeGeeQManager();
 38	manager.start();
 39	
 40	// Create event store factory
 41	BiTemporalEventStoreFactory factory = new BiTemporalEventStoreFactory(manager);
 42	
 43	// Create event store for your event type
 44	EventStore<OrderEvent> eventStore = factory.createEventStore(OrderEvent.class);
 45	```
 46	
 47	### 3. Append Events
 48	
 49	```java
 50	// Create an event
 51	OrderEvent order = new OrderEvent("ORDER-001", "CUST-123", new BigDecimal("99.99"), "CREATED");
 52	
 53	// Append with valid time (when it actually happened)
 54	Instant validTime = Instant.now().minus(1, ChronoUnit.HOURS);
 55	BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent> event = eventStore.append(
 56	 "OrderCreated", 
 57	 order, 
 58	 validTime,
 59	 Map.of("source", "web", "region", "US"),
 60	 "correlation-123",
 61	 "ORDER-001"
 62	).join();
 63	```
 64	
 65	### 4. Query Events
 66	
 67	```java
 68	// Query all events
 69	List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> allEvents = eventStore.query(EventQuery.all()).join();
 70	
 71	// Query by event type
 72	List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> orderEvents = eventStore.query(
 73	 EventQuery.forEventType("OrderCreated")
 74	).join();
 75	
 76	// Query by aggregate
 77	List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> order1Events = eventStore.query(
 78	 EventQuery.forAggregate("ORDER-001")
 79	).join();
 80	
 81	// Temporal range query
 82	List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> recentEvents = eventStore.query(
 83	 EventQuery.builder()
 84	 .validTimeRange(TemporalRange.from(Instant.now().minus(24, ChronoUnit.HOURS)))
 85	 .sortOrder(EventQuery.SortOrder.VALID_TIME_DESC)
 86	 .limit(100)
 87	 .build()
 88	).join();
 89	```
 90	
 91	### 5. Event Corrections
 92	
 93	```java
 94	// Append a correction for a previous event
 95	OrderEvent correctedOrder = new OrderEvent("ORDER-001", "CUST-123", new BigDecimal("89.99"), "CREATED");
 96	
 97	BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent> correction = eventStore.appendCorrection(
 98	 originalEvent.getEventId(),
 99	 "OrderCreated",
 100	 correctedOrder,
 101	 validTime,
 102	 "Price correction due to discount"
 103	).join();
 104	
 105	// Get all versions of an event
 106	List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> versions = eventStore.getAllVersions(originalEvent.getEventId()).join();
 107	```
 108	
 109	### 6. Point-in-Time Queries
 110	
 111	```java
 112	// Get event as it existed at a specific transaction time
 113	Instant pointInTime = Instant.now().minus(1, ChronoUnit.HOURS);
 114	BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent> historicalEvent = eventStore.getAsOfTransactionTime(
 115	 eventId, 
 116	 pointInTime
 117	).join();
 118	
 119	// Query events as they were valid at a specific time
 120	List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> historicalView = eventStore.query(
 121	 EventQuery.asOfValidTime(pointInTime)
 122	).join();
 123	```
 124	
 125	### 7. Real-time Subscriptions
 126	
 127	```java
 128	// Subscribe to all events
 129	eventStore.subscribe(null, event -> {
 130	 System.out.println("New event: " + event.getEventType());
 131	 return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null);
 132	}).join();
 133	
 134	// Subscribe to specific event type
 135	eventStore.subscribe("OrderCreated", event -> {
 136	 System.out.println("New order: " + event.getPayload());
 137	 return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null);
 138	}).join();
 139	
 140	// Subscribe to events for specific aggregate
 141	eventStore.subscribe("OrderCreated", "ORDER-001", event -> {
 142	 System.out.println("Order 001 updated: " + event.getPayload());
 143	 return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null);
 144	}).join();
 145	```

 147	## Database Schema
 148	
 149	The bi-temporal event store uses a dedicated table with the following structure:
 150	
 151	```sql
 152	CREATE TABLE bitemporal_event_log (
 153	 id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
 154	 event_id VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
 155	 event_type VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
 156	 
 157	 -- Bi-temporal dimensions
 158	 valid_time TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NOT NULL,
 159	 transaction_time TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT NOW() NOT NULL,
 160	 
 161	 -- Event data
 162	 payload JSONB NOT NULL,
 163	 headers JSONB DEFAULT '{}',
 164	 
 165	 -- Versioning and corrections
 166	 version BIGINT DEFAULT 1 NOT NULL,
 167	 previous_version_id VARCHAR(255),
 168	 is_correction BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE NOT NULL,
 169	 correction_reason TEXT,
 170	 
 171	 -- Grouping and correlation
 172	 correlation_id VARCHAR(255),
 173	 aggregate_id VARCHAR(255),
 174	 
 175	 -- Metadata
 176	 created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT NOW() NOT NULL
 177	);
 178	```
 179	
 180	## Temporal Concepts
 181	
 182	### Valid Time vs Transaction Time
 183	
 184	- **Valid Time**: When the event actually happened in the real world (business time)
 185	- **Transaction Time**: When the event was recorded in the system (system time)
 186	
 187	This bi-temporal approach allows you to:
 188	- Correct historical data while maintaining audit trails
 189	- Query data as it was known at any point in time
 190	- Handle late-arriving events correctly
 191	- Support regulatory compliance and auditing requirements
 192	
 193	### Event Versioning
 194	
 195	Events can be corrected by creating new versions:
 196	- Original event: version 1, is_correction = false
 197	- Correction: version 2, is_correction = true, previous_version_id = original_event_id
 198	- Each correction creates a new event with incremented version
 199

 37	/**
 38	 * Comprehensive example demonstrating the bi-temporal event store capabilities.
 39	 * 
 40	 * This example shows:
 41	 * - Append-only event storage with bi-temporal dimensions
 42	 * - Event corrections and versioning
 43	 * - Historical queries and point-in-time views
 44	 * - Real-time event subscriptions
 45	 * - Type-safe event handling
 46	 * 
 47	 * @author Mark Andrew Ray-Smith Cityline Ltd
 48	 * @since 2025-07-15
 49	 * @version 1.0
 50	 */
 51	public class BiTemporalEventStoreExample {
 52	 
 53	 private static final Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(BiTemporalEventStoreExample.class);
 54	 
 55	 /**
 56	 * Example event payload representing an order.
 57	 */
 58	 public static class OrderEvent {
 59	 private final String orderId;
 60	 private final String customerId;
 61	 private final BigDecimal amount;
 62	 private final String status;
 63	 
 64	 @JsonCreator
 65	 public OrderEvent(@JsonProperty("orderId") String orderId,
 66	 @JsonProperty("customerId") String customerId,
 67	 @JsonProperty("amount") BigDecimal amount,
 68	 @JsonProperty("status") String status) {
 69	 this.orderId = orderId;
 70	 this.customerId = customerId;
 71	 this.amount = amount;
 72	 this.status = status;
 73	 }
 74	 
 75	 public String getOrderId() { return orderId; }
 76	 public String getCustomerId() { return customerId; }
 77	 public BigDecimal getAmount() { return amount; }
 78	 public String getStatus() { return status; }
 79	 
 80	 @Override
 81	 public boolean equals(Object o) {
 82	 if (this == o) return true;
 83	 if (o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()) return false;
 84	 OrderEvent that = (OrderEvent) o;
 85	 return Objects.equals(orderId, that.orderId) &&
 86	 Objects.equals(customerId, that.customerId) &&
 87	 Objects.equals(amount, that.amount) &&
 88	 Objects.equals(status, that.status);
 89	 }
 90	 
 91	 @Override
 92	 public int hashCode() {
 93	 return Objects.hash(orderId, customerId, amount, status);
 94	 }
 95	 
 96	 @Override
 97	 public String toString() {
 98	 return "OrderEvent{" +
 99	 "orderId='" + orderId + '\'' +
 100	 ", customerId='" + customerId + '\'' +
 101	 ", amount=" + amount +
 102	 ", status='" + status + '\'' +
 103	 '}';
 104	 }
 105	 }
 106	 
 107	 public static void main(String[] args) {
 108	 logger.info("Starting Bi-Temporal Event Store Example");
 109	 
 110	 // Start PostgreSQL container
 111	 try (PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:15")
 112	 .withDatabaseName("peegeeq_test")
 113	 .withUsername("test")
 114	 .withPassword("test")) {
 115	 
 116	 postgres.start();
 117	 logger.info("PostgreSQL container started on port: {}", postgres.getFirstMappedPort());
 118	 
 119	 // Set system properties for PeeGeeQ configuration
 120	 System.setProperty("peegeeq.database.host", postgres.getHost());
 121	 System.setProperty("peegeeq.database.port", String.valueOf(postgres.getFirstMappedPort()));
 122	 System.setProperty("peegeeq.database.name", postgres.getDatabaseName());
 123	 System.setProperty("peegeeq.database.username", postgres.getUsername());
 124	 System.setProperty("peegeeq.database.password", postgres.getPassword());
 125	
 126	 // Configure PeeGeeQ
 127	 PeeGeeQConfiguration config = new PeeGeeQConfiguration();
 128	 
 129	 // Initialize PeeGeeQ
 130	 try (PeeGeeQManager manager = new PeeGeeQManager(config)) {
 131	 manager.start();
 132	 logger.info("PeeGeeQ Manager started successfully");
 133	 
 134	 // Create bi-temporal event store factory
 135	 BiTemporalEventStoreFactory factory = new BiTemporalEventStoreFactory(manager);
 136	 
 137	 // Create event store for OrderEvent
 138	 try (EventStore<OrderEvent> eventStore = factory.createEventStore(OrderEvent.class)) {
 139	 
 140	 // Run the example
 141	 runBiTemporalExample(eventStore).join();
 142	 
 143	 } catch (Exception e) {
 144	 logger.error("Error in bi-temporal example: {}", e.getMessage(), e);
 145	 }
 146	 
 147	 } catch (Exception e) {
 148	 logger.error("Error with PeeGeeQ Manager: {}", e.getMessage(), e);
 149	 }
 150	 
 151	 } catch (Exception e) {
 152	 logger.error("Error with PostgreSQL container: {}", e.getMessage(), e);
 153	 }
 154	 
 155	 logger.info("Bi-Temporal Event Store Example completed");
 156	 }
 157	 
 158	 private static CompletableFuture<Void> runBiTemporalExample(EventStore<OrderEvent> eventStore) {
 159	 return CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> {
 160	 try {
 161	 logger.info("=== Bi-Temporal Event Store Example ===");
 162	 
 163	 // 1. Append initial events
 164	 logger.info("\n1. Appending initial events...");
 165	 
 166	 Instant baseTime = Instant.now().minus(1, ChronoUnit.HOURS);
 167	 
 168	 OrderEvent order1 = new OrderEvent("ORDER-001", "CUST-123", 
 169	 new BigDecimal("99.99"), "CREATED");
 170	 OrderEvent order2 = new OrderEvent("ORDER-002", "CUST-456", 
 171	 new BigDecimal("149.99"), "CREATED");
 172	 
 173	 BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent> event1 = eventStore.append(
 174	 "OrderCreated", order1, baseTime,
 175	 Map.of("source", "web", "region", "US"),
 176	 "corr-001", "ORDER-001"
 177	 ).join();
 178	 
 179	 BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent> event2 = eventStore.append(
 180	 "OrderCreated", order2, baseTime.plus(10, ChronoUnit.MINUTES),
 181	 Map.of("source", "mobile", "region", "EU"),
 182	 "corr-002", "ORDER-002"
 183	 ).join();
 184	 
 185	 logger.info("Created event 1: {}", event1.getEventId());
 186	 logger.info("Created event 2: {}", event2.getEventId());
 187	 
 188	 // 2. Query all events
 189	 logger.info("\n2. Querying all events...");
 190	 
 191	 List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> allEvents = eventStore.query(EventQuery.all()).join();
 192	 logger.info("Found {} events:", allEvents.size());
 193	 for (BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent> event : allEvents) {
 194	 logger.info(" Event: {} - {} - {}", 
 195	 event.getEventId(), event.getEventType(), event.getPayload());
 196	 }
 197	 
 198	 // 3. Query by event type
 199	 logger.info("\n3. Querying by event type...");
 200	 
 201	 List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> orderEvents = eventStore.query(
 202	 EventQuery.forEventType("OrderCreated")
 203	 ).join();
 204	 logger.info("Found {} OrderCreated events", orderEvents.size());
 205	 
 206	 // 4. Query by aggregate
 207	 logger.info("\n4. Querying by aggregate...");
 208	 
 209	 List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> order1Events = eventStore.query(
 210	 EventQuery.forAggregate("ORDER-001")
 211	 ).join();
 212	 logger.info("Found {} events for ORDER-001", order1Events.size());
 213	 
 214	 // 5. Add a correction event
 215	 logger.info("\n5. Adding correction event...");
 216	 
 217	 OrderEvent correctedOrder = new OrderEvent("ORDER-001", "CUST-123", 
 218	 new BigDecimal("89.99"), "CREATED");
 219	 
 220	 BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent> correctionEvent = eventStore.appendCorrection(
 221	 event1.getEventId(), "OrderCreated", correctedOrder, baseTime,
 222	 Map.of("source", "web", "region", "US", "corrected", "true"),
 223	 "corr-001", "ORDER-001", "Price correction due to discount"
 224	 ).join();
 225	 
 226	 logger.info("Created correction event: {}", correctionEvent.getEventId());
 227	 
 228	 // 6. Get all versions of an event
 229	 logger.info("\n6. Getting all versions of ORDER-001 event...");
 230	 
 231	 List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> versions = eventStore.getAllVersions(event1.getEventId()).join();
 232	 logger.info("Found {} versions:", versions.size());
 233	 for (BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent> version : versions) {
 234	 logger.info(" Version {}: {} - Correction: {}", 
 235	 version.getVersion(), version.getPayload().getAmount(), 
 236	 version.isCorrection());
 237	 }
 238	 
 239	 // 7. Point-in-time query (as of transaction time)
 240	 logger.info("\n7. Point-in-time query (before correction)...");
 241	 
 242	 Instant beforeCorrection = correctionEvent.getTransactionTime().minus(1, ChronoUnit.SECONDS);
 243	 BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent> eventBeforeCorrection = eventStore.getAsOfTransactionTime(
 244	 event1.getEventId(), beforeCorrection
 245	 ).join();
 246	 
 247	 if (eventBeforeCorrection != null) {
 248	 logger.info("Event before correction: {} (amount: {})", 
 249	 eventBeforeCorrection.getEventId(), 
 250	 eventBeforeCorrection.getPayload().getAmount());
 251	 } else {
 252	 logger.info("No event found before correction time");
 253	 }
 254	 
 255	 // 8. Temporal range query
 256	 logger.info("\n8. Temporal range query...");
 257	 
 258	 Instant rangeStart = baseTime.minus(30, ChronoUnit.MINUTES);
 259	 Instant rangeEnd = baseTime.plus(30, ChronoUnit.MINUTES);
 260	 
 261	 List<BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent>> rangeEvents = eventStore.query(
 262	 EventQuery.builder()
 263	 .validTimeRange(new TemporalRange(rangeStart, rangeEnd))
 264	 .sortOrder(EventQuery.SortOrder.VALID_TIME_ASC)
 265	 .build()
 266	 ).join();
 267	 
 268	 logger.info("Found {} events in time range:", rangeEvents.size());
 269	 for (BiTemporalEvent<OrderEvent> event : rangeEvents) {
 270	 logger.info(" Event: {} at {}", 
 271	 event.getPayload().getOrderId(), event.getValidTime());
 272	 }
 273	 
 274	 // 9. Get statistics
 275	 logger.info("\n9. Getting event store statistics...");
 276	 
 277	 EventStore.EventStoreStats stats = eventStore.getStats().join();
 278	 logger.info("Event Store Statistics:");
 279	 logger.info(" Total events: {}", stats.getTotalEvents());
 280	 logger.info(" Total corrections: {}", stats.getTotalCorrections());
 281	 logger.info(" Event counts by type: {}", stats.getEventCountsByType());
 282	 logger.info(" Oldest event time: {}", stats.getOldestEventTime());
 283	 logger.info(" Newest event time: {}", stats.getNewestEventTime());
 284	 logger.info(" Storage size: {} bytes", stats.getStorageSizeBytes());
 285	 
 286	 logger.info("\n=== Bi-Temporal Event Store Example Completed Successfully ===");
 287	 
 288	 } catch (Exception e) {
 289	 logger.error("Error in bi-temporal example: {}", e.getMessage(), e);
 290	 throw new RuntimeException(e);
 291	 }
 292	 });

 498	 /**
 499	 * Gracefully shuts down an executor service with proper timeout handling.
 500	 */
 501	 private void shutdownExecutorGracefully(ExecutorService executor, String name) {
 502	 logger.debug("Shutting down executor: {}", name);
 503	
 504	 executor.shutdown();
 505	
 506	 try {
 507	 if (!executor.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
 508	 logger.warn("Executor {} did not terminate gracefully, forcing shutdown", name);
 509	 executor.shutdownNow();
 510	
 511	 if (!executor.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
 512	 logger.error("Executor {} did not terminate after forced shutdown", name);
 513	 } else {
 514	 logger.debug("Executor {} terminated after forced shutdown", name);
 515	 }
 516	 } else {
 517	 logger.debug("Executor {} terminated gracefully", name);
 518	 }
 519	 } catch (InterruptedException e) {
 520	 logger.warn("Interrupted while shutting down executor {}", name);
 521	 executor.shutdownNow();
 522	 Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
 523	 }
 524	 }
 525	}

 25	 * Bi-temporal events track two time dimensions:

 28	 *

 43	 *
 44	 * @return The event ID
 45	 */
 46	 String getEventId();

 48	 /**
 49	 * Gets the event type identifier.

 52	 * @return The event type

 54	 String getEventType();
